column2: Nakula, his horses slain, tormented by Karna's son, leapt from Bhima's chariot, as a lion to a mountain peak, in Dhananjaya's sight.

Knowing Nakula chariotless, with bow, arrows and sword cut, afflicted by foes' arrows and broken by the weapons of Karna's son, those chariots, with fluttering pennants, thundering, with prancing horses, driven by the best men, swiftly came on.

The five best of Drupada's sons, with Shaineya as sixth, and the five sons of Drupada's daughter, enduring foes, slaying your elephants, chariots, men and horses with arrows like the lords of serpents, weapons in hand,

then your chief chariot-warriors hastened to meet them—Hridika's son, Kripa, Drona's son, Duryodhana, Shakuni, Shuka, Vrika, Kratha and Devavridha—with the thunder of elephants and clouds, chariots and bows.

Your foremost heroes struck and surrounded those ten and one with the best of excellent arrows; the Kunindas came against them with elephants dark as new clouds, like mountain peaks, of terrible speed.
Well equipped, intoxicated Himalayan elephants, ridden by skilled men eager for battle and covered with golden nets, shone like clouds with lightning.
The Kuninda prince tormented Kripa with his charioteer and horses greatly with ten great iron arrows; then, struck by the arrows of Sharadvat's son, he fell to the ground with his elephant.
The Kuninda prince's younger brother, with iron javelins bright as sunbeams, roared, shaking Kripa's chariot, and then the lord of Gandhara cut off his head.
Then, when those Kunindas were slain, your great chariot-warriors, delighted, blew their conches born of the salt sea and, bows in hand, advanced on the enemy.
Then a most dreadful battle again took place between the Kurus and the Pandavas with the Srinjayas, with swords, darts, lances, maces and axes, men, horses and elephants greatly confused.
Then, struck by each other with chariots, horses, elephants and foot-soldiers, they fell to the ground like clouds with lightning and thunder, driven from all quarters by fierce winds.
Then Shatanika slew your great elephants, chariots and bands of foot-soldiers; Bhoja killed horses, and elephants fell, weaponless and cut by Kritavarman.
Then three other elephants struck by Drona's son, with all their weapons, warriors and banners, fell lifeless to the earth like great mountains struck by thunderbolts.
The next after the Kuninda king's younger brother struck your son in the chest with excellent arrows; your son pierced his body and that elephant with sharp arrows.
That king of elephants fell with the king's son, streaming much blood in all directions, like a mountain of red ochre with water, at the coming of the rains, struck by Shachi's lord's thunderbolt.
The Kuninda prince's other elephant, sent against Shuka, crushed him with his charioteer, horses and chariot; then Kratha fell, split by arrows, like a mountain struck by the lord's thunderbolt.
The lord of Kratha, hard to conquer, the chariot-warrior, was slain by arrows by the mountain-born on an elephant; he fell with his horses and charioteer like a great tree struck by a great wind.
Vrika pierced hard with twelve arrows the mountain-dwelling warrior on an elephant; then with four he crushed the swift horse Vrika, with chariot and horses, at the foot.
That king of elephants fell with its driver, struck hard by the arrows of Babhru's sons; and Devavridha's son, tormented, fell, struck by Sahadeva's son.
The Kuninda prince, wishing to kill Shakuni with an elephant that struck the limbs of the tusked ones' offspring, went swiftly, tormenting him greatly; then the lord of Gandhara cut off his head.
Then the great elephants slain by Shatanika, horses, chariots and bands of foot-soldiers of yours, helpless, fell crushed to the earth, as trees struck by Garuda's wind.
Then the Kuninda prince, smiling, pierced Nakula's son with many sharp arrows; Nakula's son cut off his head, face like a lotus, from his body with a razor-arrow.
Then Karna's son pierced Shatanika with three sharp swift arrows, Arjuna with three, Bhima with three, Nakula with seven, and Janardana with twelve arrows.
Seeing that superhuman deed of his, the Kauravas, delighted, honoured him; and those knowing Dhananjaya's prowess thought him thrown into the fire.
Then Kiriti, slayer of heroes, seeing the hero chariotless, ran at Vrishasena in battle, as he stood before the charioteer's son.
Karna's son, the great chariot-warrior, attacked that fierce hero of men, bearer of a thousand arrows in the great battle, as Namuchi attacked Indra of old.
Then the greatly noble son of the charioteer's son, piercing Partha with a hundred and one marvellous arrows, roared a roar, as Namuchi of old piercing Shakra.
Again Vrishasena pierced Partha with fierce arrows at the root of the arm, and tormented Krishna with nine, and Partha again with ten sharp-pointed arrows.
Then Kiriti, at the head of the battle, in anger making a three-lined frown on his forehead, the great-souled one loosed arrows for the slaying of the charioteer's son in the battle, O king.
He pierced him with ten arrows unerringly in his vitals by force, and cut his bow and arms with four razor-arrows and his head with fierce ones.
Struck by Partha's arrows, he fell from the chariot to the ground without arms and head, like a blossoming sala tree with leaves and great body blown from a mountain peak by wind.
Seeing his son struck by arrows and falling from the chariot, the charioteer's son, quick-working, tormented by the slaying of his son by Kiritin, went swiftly by chariot to chariot.
Radiant Karna went in his chariot to face the foes, his eyes red with fury for battle, challenging Dhananjaya.
The two chariots, bright as the sun and covered with tiger-skin, were seen meeting, like two suns come together.
White-horsed, sun-like men, tamers of foes, mounted, the two great souls shone like the moon and sun in the sky.
Seeing them, all beings, O revered one, were astonished, as for Indra and Virochana's son striving for the conquest of the three worlds.
Seeing the two chariots rushing with the roar of chariot and bowstring, palm and arrow-and-conch sounds, the kings
were astonished on seeing the banners meeting: the elephant-rope of Karna and the monkey of Kiritin.
Seeing the two chariots engaged, O Bharata, the kings raised lion-roars and many shouts of "Well done."
Hearing of the duel of those two, the warriors all around displayed the might of arms and waved their garments greatly.
Likewise all the Pandavas, gladdening Dhananjaya, made all the quarters resound with trumpets and conches.
With shouts, slaps of arms and cries, a tumult arose on every side, and the shouts of heroes at the meeting of Karna and Arjuna.
Seeing the two tigers among men on their chariots, best of chariot-warriors, holding great bows, with arrows, darts and maces,
armoured, with swords bound, white-horsed, adorned with conches, with fine quivers, both very handsome,
limbs smeared with red sandal, like two rutting bulls, like venomous serpents, like Yama and the Ender,
like Indra and Vritra enraged, radiant as sun and moon, like two cruel great planets come at the end of an age,
divine in birth, godlike, equal to gods in form, meeting—seeing Karna and Dhananjaya, tigers among men,
both holding excellent weapons, both labouring in battle, both filling the sky with the sound of their arms,
both of renowned deeds, equal in manliness and strength, both alike in battle like the lord of the immortals and Shambara,
equal in battle to Kartavirya and to Dasharathi, in valour equal to Vishnu, in battle equal to Bava,
both with white horses, O king, drawn by the best chariots, and their charioteers were both mighty,
seeing those two great chariot-warriors shining, O great king, astonishment came upon the hosts of siddhas and charanas.
Then, O best of the Bharatas, Dhritarashtra's men with their force surrounded the great-souled Karna, ornament of battle, quickly.
So too the delighted Pandavas led by Dhrishtadyumna surrounded the great-souled Partha, incomparable in battle.
On your side, in battle, Karna was the stake, O lord of men, and on the Pandavas' side Partha was the stake in the battle.
They themselves were the assembly there and the spectators; for them gambling there, victory and defeat were certain.
The gamble between them was joined for victory or the other, for us and for the Pandavas, standing at the head of the battle.
Those two stood, O great king, in the battle, practised in war, each enraged at the other, each desiring the other's defeat.
Those two wished to seize each other, like Indra and Vritra, of fearful form, like two great smoky planets.
Then in the sky there were disputes with reproaches, O best of the Bharatas, and divisions among beings between Karna and Arjuna; the quarters were divided and all worlds took sides.
Gods, danavas, gandharvas, pishachas, serpents and rakshasas took sides at the meeting of Karna and Arjuna.
Heaven with its stars was on Karna's side, O lord of men; the vast earth was on Partha's side, as mother of her son, O Bharata.
Rivers, oceans, mountains, O best of men, trees and herbs took refuge with Kiritin.
Asuras, yatudhanas and guhyakas, scorcher of foes, and sky-ranging birds were on Karna's side.
Jewels, treasures and all the Vedas with the Itihasa as fifth, with the Upavedas and Upanishads, with their secrets and summaries,
Vasuki, Chitrasena, Takshaka and Upatakshaka, and all the mountains, and the sons of Kadru with their lineages, the venomous and mightily wrathful serpents, were on Arjuna's side.
The Airavatas, Saurabheyas and Vaishaleyas, the snakes, were on Arjuna's side; the small snakes on Karna's.
Wolves, tigers, auspicious beasts and birds, O king, all took refuge with Partha's victory.
Vasus, Maruts, Sadhyas, Rudras, Vishvedevas and the Ashvins, Agni, Indra, Soma, the wind and the ten quarters went to Dhananjaya; the Adityas were on Karna's side.
The gods with the fathers were with their hosts on Arjuna's side; Yama, Vaishravana and Varuna were where Arjuna was.
The hosts of gods, Brahmanas and royal sages were on the Pandava's side; Tumburu and the gandharvas, O king, were where Arjuna was.
Pravaya with Maunaya, hosts of gandharvas and apsarases, with wolf and tiger beasts, elephants, chariots and foot-soldiers—
borne by clouds and by the wind, the wise gathered, wishing to see the meeting of Karna and Arjuna.
Gods, danavas, gandharvas, nagas, yakshas, birds, great sages knowing the Veda, and the fathers who feed on svadha,
austerities, sciences and herbs, in many forms and robes and radiance, O great king, stood in the sky, roaring.
Brahma with the Brahmin sages and the Lords of Creatures, and Bhava with them, came to that place in a divine car.
Seeing the Lord of Creatures, the gods approached the Self-existent: "Let victory be equal for these two lions among men, O God."
Hearing that, Maghavan bowed to the Grandsire: "Let the whole world not perish through the destruction of Karna and Arjuna.
Self-existent One, say that word: let victory be equal for these two." "So let it be; salutations to you; be gracious to me, Lord."
Then Brahma and Ishana said to the lord of the thirty gods, "Let the victory be sure—the victory of the great-souled Vijaya (Arjuna).
He is wise, strong, brave, skilled in weapons and rich in austerity; the greatly splendid one bears the whole science of the bow.
Through greatness he might transgress, and by the turning of fate this may happen; and if he transgresses, the destruction of the worlds would be certain.
There is no fixed limit for the two enraged Krishnas anywhere; both, best of men, are creators of the unreal and the real.
These two are Nara and Narayana, ancient best of sages, restrainers who are unrestrained, fearless, scorchers of foes.
Let Karna, best of men, gain the foremost worlds; let hero Vaikartana, brave, win; but let victory be the Krishnas'.
Let him gain the world of the Vasus or Maruts, and with Drona and Bhishma be honoured in the world of heaven."
Thus told by the two gods of gods, the thousand-eyed one, taking leave of all beings, spoke by the command of Brahma and Ishana:
You have heard what was said by the two Lords for the good of the world; so it will be, not otherwise; remain, your anger gone.
Hearing Indra's words, all beings, O revered one, were astonished, O king, and honoured it.
The gods let fall from the sky fragrant flowers in many forms and played divine instruments.
Wishing to see the incomparable duel of the two lions among men, gods, danavas and gandharvas all stayed; and those two chariots, white-horsed, with their banners yoked, of great sound.
The heroes of the world who had come blew their conches severally—the heroes Vasudeva and Arjuna, and Karna and Shalya, O Bharata.
That battle, terrifying to the timid, then took place, in rivalry of valour, like that of Shakra and Shambara.
Their banners, with garlands, shone on the chariots, differing in form, and they were angry at each other in the battle.
Karna's elephant-rope banner, bright as a serpent, jewelled, firm, shone like Indra's bow.
The best of monkeys on Partha's, gaping, terrifying, frightening with his fangs, was hard to look at as the sun.
Eager for battle, the banner of the Gandiva-bowman approached Karna's banner and roared, challenging it.
Leaping up with great speed, the monkey struck the rope with nails and teeth, as Garuda a serpent.
Enraged, the iron elephant-rope with fine little bells, like the noose of Death, rushed at the great monkey.
In that best battle of both, the duel brought as a wager, the two banners made war, and horses neighed at horses.
The lotus-eyed one (Krishna) pierced Shalya with his eye-arrows, and he looked back at the lotus-eyed one the same way.
There Vasudeva conquered Shalya with his eye-arrows, and Dhananjaya son of Kunti conquered Karna by his glance.
Then the charioteer's son, smiling, said to Shalya: "If Partha should slay me in the battle today, what would be your answer then? Tell me truly, friend."
[Shalya said:] "If, Karna, the white-horsed one slays you in the battle today, I shall slay both Madhava and the Pandava on a single chariot."
[Sanjaya said:] Arjuna spoke thus to Govinda; laughing, Krishna said these words to Partha:

The sun might fall from its place, the earth might split into many pieces, fire might become cold, but Karna would not slay you, Dhananjaya.
mahabharata:8:63.77	But if somehow it should be as a ruin of the world, I would slay Karna and Shalya with my two arms in the battle.
Hearing Krishna's words, Arjuna, the monkey-bannered, laughing, replied to Krishna of unwearied deeds: "These two, Karna and Shalya, are not even enough for me, Janardana.
Today you will see Karna with his pennant and banner, with Shalya, chariot and horses, with parasol, armour, dart, arrows and bow,
cut in many ways in the battle by my arrows; today with his chariot, horses, dart, armour and weapons—for my enmity is not quenched for his laughing at Krishna long ago.
Today you will see Karna, Govinda, uprooted by me like a flowering tree by a rutting elephant.
Today you will hear those sweet words, Madhusudana; today, free of debt, you will console Abhimanyu's mother and Kunti, my father's sister, rejoicing, Janardana.
Today you will console Krishna (Draupadi), her face in tears, Madhava, and the king of dharma Yudhishthira with words like nectar."
All the men saw in the sky those beings, wondrous in form, standing in the air, resounding with sweet sounds, with instruments, songs, praises and dances.
Then, delighted, the Kuru and Pandava warriors, with the sounds of instruments, leaves, weapons and lion-roars, making the earth and quarters resound, struck their foes with a roar.

The battlefield, crowded with tens of thousands of horses, elephants and chariots of many kinds, hard to bear for the fall of swords, darts and lances, frequented by the fearless, thronged with slain bodies, shone red with blood.
As the battle of weapon-bearers' defeat went on, Dhananjaya and Adhiratha's son, armoured, covered the quarters and the armies with sharp straight arrows.
Then, with a darkness made by arrows, yours and the enemy knew nothing; in fear they took refuge in those very two chariots, which dispelled the darkness like rays spread in the sky.
Then, those two, warding off each other's weapon with weapon, like winds from east and west in a dense darkness of cloud spread out, shone exceedingly like risen suns.
They are not to be approached—so urged, the enemy and yours stood around those two great chariot-warriors on every side, as gods and asuras around Vasava and Shambara.
With the sounds of mridangas, kettledrums, tabors, anakas and conches, with lion-roars, the two best of men shone like moon and sun amid a deluge of clouds.
Then those two great bowmen, loosing great weapons with terrible arrows, killed countless men, horses and elephants and struck each other with the best of arrows.

Then, tormented by arrows from the two best of men, the supporters of Kurus and Pandavas scattered with elephants, foot-soldiers, horses and chariots in all directions, like forest dwellers from fear of a lion.
Then Duryodhana, Bhoja, Subala's son, and Kripa with Sharadvat's son, five great chariot-warriors, struck Dhananjaya and Achyuta with body-ending arrows.
Dhananjaya cut their bows, quivers, horses, banners, chariots and charioteers all together with arrows, pierced them, and pierced the charioteer's son with twelve of the best arrows.
Then a hundred chariots and a hundred elephants, aggressors, rushed hastily at Arjuna—Shakas, Tukharas, Yavanas, horsemen with the best of Kambojas, wishing to kill him.
Dhananjaya in haste cut with razor-arrows the excellent weapons in their hands with their hands and their heads, and horses, elephants and chariots of the fighters; he destroyed that host of foes.
Then in the sky, sounds of divine trumpets with shouts of "Well done" sent by the delighted, and showers of the finest flowers fell, fragrant, lovely and auspicious, driven by the wind.
Seeing that wonder, witnessed by gods and men, beings were astonished, O king; but your son and the charioteer's son felt neither pain nor wonder, being of one resolve.
Then Drona's son, pressing your son's hand with his hand to console him, said, "Be gracious, Duryodhana; make peace with the Pandavas; enough of enmity; fie on war.
The preceptor, equal to Brahma, knower of great weapons, has been slain, and Bhishma and the other best of men; I am safe, and so is my uncle; rule your kingdom long with the Pandavas.
Dhananjaya will stand when I hold him back; Janardana wishes no enmity; Yudhishthira is ever intent on the good of beings, and Vrikodara and the twins follow him.
Between you and the Parthas let the people have peace; let the remaining kings go each to his own city, and let the soldiers cease their enmity."

If you do not listen to my word, O king, you will surely be tormented, slain by your foes in battle; and the world has seen with you what was done by the single Kiritin, as neither Death nor Indra nor Prachetas nor the king of the yakshas would do.
mahabharata:8:64.25	He is superior in qualities even to that, Dhananjaya; he will accept my whole word and will follow you; be gracious, O king, for the peace of the world.
mahabharata:8:64.26	My pride in you is ever supreme; I tell you so out of the highest friendship, and I shall hold back even Karna when you are willing.
mahabharata:8:64.27	The wise call a friend innate; so too one gained by conciliation, by wealth, or by coming through valour—all four kinds exist in you and the Pandavas.
mahabharata:8:64.28	By nature your kinsmen, hero; again gain them firmly by conciliation; if with you pleased they become friends, O lord of lords, surely do so.
Thus addressed by his friend with wholesome words, he reflected, sighed and said, dejected: "It is as you say, friend; yet hear my word as I tell you.
Having slain Duhshasana, the evil-minded Vrikodara spoke much, like a tiger, by force; that stays in my heart; it is not hidden from you; whence peace?
Nor, Achyuta, should you speak to Karna to desist out of praise of Drona's son; Phalguna is today exhausted by great labour; Karna will slay him by splendour."
Having consoled him thus repeatedly, your son commanded his own soldiers: "Strike, rush at these foes with the sound of arrows; why remain silent?"
As two Himalayan elephants in rut, like two tusked elephants for a cow in season, so the heroes Dhananjaya and Adhiratha's son met with fierce speed.
As cloud with cloud, or by chance mountain with mountain, so those two, with the sound of bowstring, palm and wheel-rims, showering arrows, came together.
Like mountains with tall peaks, trees, creepers and herbs, mountains with many kinds of dwellers, or two mighty falling mountains, they struck each other with great weapons.
Their encounter was great, as of old between the lord of gods and Virochana's son; with charioteers, horses and bodies broken by arrows, hard to bear for others, with blood for water.
Like two great lakes with abundant lotuses and blue lotuses, fish and tortoises, resounding with hosts of birds and stirred together by a wind, so the two bannered chariots met.
Both equal in valour to Mahendra, both great chariot-warriors like Mahendra, they struck each other with arrows like Mahendra's thunderbolt, as Mahendra and Vritra.

Both armies with elephants, foot-soldiers, horses and chariots, with garments, ornaments and garlands of many colours, trembled and rose up in wonder; and those in the sky at the fight of Arjuna and Karna.
Arms with fingers like thunderbolts were raised with lion-roars by delighted watchers when Adhiratha's son advanced on Arjuna wishing to kill him, as a rutting elephant on an elephant.
Then Karna first pierced Partha there with ten great arrows; Arjuna pierced him back with sharp-pointed ones in the armpit with ten, exceedingly enraged.
Those two hewed each other with very sharp arrows, the charioteer's son and Arjuna, each seeking the other's weak point, delighted in the crush, going to the very fearful.

Unable to bear it in the great battle, the great-souled Bhimasena grew angry there; he said, striking hand on hand, biting his lip, dancing as it were and beating time: "How has the charioteer's son pierced you, Kiritin, in front with ten great arrows?
With the resolve by which you conquered all beings and gave food to fire at Khandava, with that resolve slay the charioteer's son; or I shall crush him with my mace."
Then Vasudeva said to Partha, seeing the arrows being struck down, "Karna crushes your weapons with weapons in every way today; what is this, Kiritin?
Hero, why are you bewildered, not attending? These Kauravas roar, greatly delighted; all know Karna honoured, and your weapon felled by weapons.
With the resolve by which the Tamasa weapon was slain, and the dreadful rakshasas in age after age and the asuras born of pride in the battles, with that resolve slay the charioteer's son.
With this razor-edged discus today cut off the foe's head by force; by my released Sudarshana, as Shakra with the thunderbolt cut Namuchi, the foe.
With the great resolve by which the Lord in the form of a Kirata was pleased by you, take that resolve again and slay the charioteer's son with his followers.
Then give the earth to the king, girdled by the sea, with cities and villages, prosperous, with the hosts of foes slain, and gain incomparable fame, Partha."
Urged thus by Bhima and Janardana, remembering himself and looking to his own strength, and knowing the purpose of the great soul's coming, he said to Keshava:

I bring forth a fierce great weapon, for the welfare of the world and for the slaying of the charioteer's son. Permit me, you and the gods, Brahma, the Brahmins of the earth and all knowers of Brahman.

Having said so, he brought forth the unbearable Brahma weapon to be directed by mind; then he covered all quarters and intermediate quarters with arrows of great splendour. The best of the Bharatas loosed hundreds upon hundreds of swift arrows.
By Vaikartana also in the battle thousands of masses of arrows were loosed; roaring, they approached the Pandava like streams of rain loosed from a cloud.
Of superhuman deed, of Bhima-like strength, he struck Bhimasena, Janardana and Kiritin with three each and roared a dreadful roar with a great voice.
Struck by Karna's arrows, Kiriti, seeing Bhima and Janardana, unable to bear it, Partha again drew forth eighteen arrows.
Piercing Sushena with one arrow, and Shalya with four and Karna with three, he then struck down with ten well-loosed arrows the golden-armoured chief of the assembly.
The prince, without head, arms, horses, charioteer, bow or banner, fell from the front of the chariot, shattered, like a sala tree cut by axes.
Again piercing Karna with three, eight, two, four and ten, he slew four hundred armed elephants, eight hundred chariots, a thousand horses, again horsemen, and eight thousand foot-soldiers.
Seeing the two best fighters, slayers of foes, engaged in battle, those in the sky and those on earth stood, wishing to see, when Karna and Partha had reined in their horses.
Weeping, the charioteer, O Janamejaya, said to the king, not glad at heart, in a voice choked with tears:
The sky, adorned with scattered planets, stars and constellations, seemed on every side like a cloth to behold.
The word of the aged Bhishma, of Gandhari and of Vidura was not followed by your son, O Bharata.
Neither Partha, the white-horsed one, nor I nor Bhima nor the twins knew that brother; but he of good vows knew us.
[The hunter said:] "Many should be protected by one; one should not be protected for many, Gautami; the knowers of dharma abandon the offender; kill this crawling sinner."
You have heard the royal duties from Bhishma, son of Bhagirathi, from Krishna Dvaipayana, from Narada and from Vidura.
That did not leave the heart of the ill-minded Dhritarashtra—what was brought about by the dice.
By the king's order the men cast it into the sea, and proclaimed in the city at Ahuka's command.
Chitrangada went to Manipura; the other mothers surrounded Parikshit.
Shikhandin the Panchala, the sons of Draupadi in full, and the invincible Abhimanyu—I wish to see them, Narada.
